edition: Issue 050: Fonterra wants permission to dump 22 million litres of milk while we're still paying over $5 a bottle, the US ambassador and Auckland's mayor are in a public stoush that's solving nothing, and the Black Caps 'got away with' a draw that feels like a win
tagline: Your 3-minute Tuesday reset: the dairy giant having a better time than your supermarket run, the diplomatic beef that escalated into name-calling, and the cricket team treating survival like the victory lap.

stories.headline: Fonterra wants consent to dump up to 22 million litres of milk — while Kiwis keep paying over $5 a bottle
stories.summary: The dairy co-op has applied to vary seven Canterbury resource consents so it can legally dispose of up to 22 million litres of surplus raw milk if factories can't process it; environmentalists, Consumer NZ and Eat NZ ask why a country producing billions of litres of milk still sees families struggling to afford it.

body.text: Fonterra has applied to vary seven resource consents in Canterbury so it can dispose of up to 22 million litres of surplus raw milk — by spreading it on farmland or irrigating it onto pasture — if its factories cannot process everything collected during peak production. The applications were filed with the Canterbury Regional Council on 2 October. The co-op says the move is precautionary: it has not needed to dispose of milk this season, and upgrades to its manufacturing network plus $1bn of South Island investment have helped it manage supply. Disposal would only ever be considered after shifting production between factories or changing what it manufactures. But the optics are hard to ignore in a country that produced roughly 3.2 million tonnes of milk in October alone yet where milk has been reported at more than $5 a bottle. Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen points to the huge seasonal swing — 3.2 million tonnes in October against about 274,000 tonnes in June — meaning extra capacity for a brief peak would cost millions and likely sit idle. Consumer NZ calls disposal an 'absolute last resort'; Eat New Zealand says the food system has become 'so specialised, consolidated and financialised' that the country could dispose of surplus while nearly one in three households faced food insecurity in the past year.

Let's just sit with the headline for a second: up to twenty-two million litres. That's a milk lake. Enough dairy to tip over a small-town water tower, bubbling gently in the Canterbury sun — while across town someone is putting the bottle back on the shelf because it's north of five dollars. The co-op has a perfectly reasonable, mind-numbingly technical explanation, and none of it makes the 'why is my milk expensive?' question sting any less when the answer involves a seasonal production curve and a co-operative that can't be bothered pouring an extra glass. Funny how the same maths that cannot stretch to a few extra processing days has no trouble at all stretching to a 22-million-litre emergency sprinkler system. Eat New Zealand's verdict — too specialised, consolidated and financialised to feed the country that farms it — is the polite way of saying we've built an industry that would rather irrigate the paddock than the pantry. Would one week of cheap milk fix the cost-of-living crisis? No, says the economist. But it would have been really nice to scroll past a headline that didn't make buying dairy feel like a political loyalty test.

Stuff (23 Nov 2026, Mildred Armah, 'Fonterra could dump 22 million litres of milk. So why are Kiwis paying so much?'): Fonterra applied to vary seven Canterbury resource consents (filed with the Canterbury Regional Council on 2 Oct 2026) to allow up to 22 million litres of surplus raw milk to be spread on farmland or irrigated onto pasture in emergencies; the co-op has not needed to dispose of milk this season and says upgrades to its manufacturing network have helped it manage supply. Brad Olsen (Infometrics principal economist): about 3.2 million tonnes of milk produced nationally in October vs about 274,000 tonnes in June; additional peak capacity would cost millions and 'might sit unused for much of the year'. Consumer NZ spokesperson: 'We... would expect that dumping 22 million litres of raw milk would be an absolute last resort'; processing capacity, not raw milk supply, is 'a more influential factor on the price consumers ultimately pay'. Eat New Zealand: the food system is 'so specialised, consolidated and financialised' that surplus milk could be disposed of while nearly one in three households experienced food insecurity in the past year (Stuff, 'one in three households struggled with food in the past year'). Fonterra has announced $1bn investment across its South Island manufacturing network over three years and says it has 24 manufacturing sites nationwide; milk prices 'more than $5 a bottle' per recent Stuff food-price reporting referenced in the article.

stories.headline: US ambassador says he 'likes to add humour to the job' — after calling Wayne Brown maybe-on-crack, a boomer, and short on intelligence
stories.summary: American ambassador Jared Novelly has again refused to back down over his criticism of Auckland mayor Wayne Brown — who told Stuff 'democracy's had its day' after a China trip — saying he 'likes to add humour to the job' and could not let Brown's Five Eyes comments stand; Labour MP Willie Jackson called Novelly a 'clown' and suggested he be kicked out.

body.text: The diplomatic tiff between the United States ambassador and Auckland's mayor shows no sign of cooling. Last week Jared Novelly said Brown 'might have been on crack' after Brown told Stuff — fresh back from a trip to China — that 'democracy's had its day' and it was time for 'something else'. Brown later clarified he was 'speaking to the fact that MMP isn't perfect'. Novelly doubled down, calling Brown a 'boomer' and questioning his intelligence in a social media post, and also demanded Brown apologise over comments made to a Chinese state broadcaster in which he suggested New Zealand should leave Five Eyes and 'sell our seat to Japan'. On Monday Novelly again stood by his remarks, saying on X that he 'likes to add humour to the job' and 'that's just who I am', while adding he 'could not let' Brown's statements on Five Eyes stand 'without countering', citing NZSIS reporting that China conducts espionage 'at scale' in New Zealand. The mayor's office declined to comment. Labour MP Willie Jackson called Novelly a 'clown' and said he should be kicked out or made to apologise; Labour's foreign affairs spokesperson Vanushi Walters said Jackson's comments did not represent party policy. Both caretaker PM Christopher Luxon and caretaker foreign minister Winston Peters declined to comment, and China's embassy accused Novelly of sowing division.

In the great tradition of New Zealand–US diplomatic incidents, this round features a mayor who declared democracy over after a business trip to China ('spoken to by the least democratic country on Earth, emerges suggesting we sell Five Eyes to Japan' — a full itinerary, Wayne) and an ambassador whose defence is that he is, at heart, a funny guy. 'I like to add humour to the job' is the sentence you reach for after your material involved an accusation of drug use, a generation slur and a formal finding that a public official is below the intelligence line. Admire the escalation ladder: crack, boomer, then a lecture on which briefings a mayor has not made the cut for. Meanwhile the actual job — the alliance, the trade, the open borders — has gone so quiet you can't hear either of them doing it. The most on-brand detail: one Labour MP calls the ambassador a clown, the ambassador says he likes humour, and the two caretaker politicians actually meant to manage this are delivering a textbook 'declined to comment' shuffle. The refined diplomatic conclusion is that New Zealand's democracy has, indeed, had quite a day — and it spent it arguing about what a mayor told China's state broadcaster.

Stuff (22 Nov 2026, Sam Smith, 'I like to add humour to the job': US ambassador doubles down again on Wayne Brown): last week ambassador Jared Novelly said Brown 'might have been on crack' after Brown told Stuff that 'democracy's had its day' and it was time for 'something else'; Brown later told The Post he was 'speaking to the fact that MMP isn't perfect'. Novelly also called Brown a 'boomer' and questioned his intelligence, saying 'it's obvious from his statements the mayor hasn't made the cut' for an intelligence briefing. Novelly demanded an apology over Brown's comments to a Chinese state broadcaster suggesting NZ leave Five Eyes and 'sell our seat to Japan': 'All Five Eyes partners should be offended, including New Zealanders.' On Monday Novelly stood by his remarks on X: 'I like to add humour to the job' and 'that's just who I am', adding he 'could not let' Brown's statements stand 'without countering', citing an August NZSIS report that China is the only nation conducting espionage 'at scale' in NZ, before saying he was 'moving on now'. Labour MP Willie Jackson called Novelly a 'clown' and said 'kick this ambassador out or get the Government to ask him for an apology'; Labour's Vanushi Walters said Jackson's comments were not party policy. Caretaker PM Christopher Luxon and caretaker foreign minister Winston Peters declined to comment; the mayor's office declined further comment; China's embassy accused Novelly of sowing division.

stories.headline: 'One we've probably got away with': Black Caps hold on for a draw against India — and Tom Latham calls it a win
stories.summary: New Zealand denied India victory in the first Test at Wellington, finishing 239-5 after an Indian first innings of 720-9 declared and a 352-run lead, with Daryl Mitchell (49 no) and Glenn Phillips (26 no) batting out almost two sessions; captain Tom Latham admitted 'that's one that we've probably got away with' but said it felt like a win.

body.text: The Black Caps have batted their way out of a very deep hole to deny India victory in the first Test in Wellington, the match ending in a draw on a windy fifth day at the Basin Reserve. India declared their single innings at 720-9 — a lead of 352 — and needed only five more wickets to win when the fifth morning began. New Zealand started the day at 119-2 and took 18 balls to score their first run; overnight batters Devon Conway (65) and Rachin Ravindra (37) fell in quick succession, leaving the hosts 157-4 at lunch and 239-5 when the captains shook hands with the hosts still 113 runs behind. Daryl Mitchell, 49 not out from 186 balls, and first-innings centurion Glenn Phillips, 26 not out from 126, put on 63 for the sixth wicket and held off India for almost two sessions. Captain Tom Latham, who bagged a pair — dismissed by Jasprit Bumrah in the first over of each innings — admitted: 'I guess that's one that we've probably got away with. Looking at the position we were in on day one... we were certainly pretty happy (with that).' The draw cost New Zealand a place in the World Test Championship standings — they started the Test on top, were overhauled by champions South Africa, and slip to third behind Australia — with the second and final Test starting Friday in Christchurch.

Let's be precise about what counted as 'success' on Monday: New Zealand survived. That's it. That's the win. After a first innings that had us five down before we'd understood it was a Test, the triumphant coda was batting out 120 overs and shaking hands with the scoreboard still open like a wound. Tom Latham, whose own batting contribution this Test was the rare and collectible double-ducks, has graded it accurately — 'that's one we've probably got away with' — and then, because he is contractually the captain, called it a win. And honestly? Fine. Earlier in this match the same ground put us 70-5 on day one, and the deep-seated New Zealand instinct is to be eight hundred runs behind and treat a draw like a trophy. Bowl a bit, defend a lot, describe the whole thing in the tone you use when the house burned down but the insurance came through. It's not the win we ordered, but it's the win we got, it's the sort of week we're living in — so by all means celebrate the draw, gently, and remember the second Test is Friday, and Bumrah will probably be rested and therefore angrier. Hold that line, fellas. Make us proud, one ball at a time.

RNZ (23 Nov 2026, 'Black Caps deny India victory in first test by holding on to last five wickets'): the first Test at Wellington's Basin Reserve ended in a draw; India declared at 720-9 for a lead of 352; NZ began day five at 119-2 and took 18 balls for their first run of the morning; Devon Conway caught behind for 65 and Rachin Ravindra out for 37; 157-4 at lunch; Tom Blundell out six overs after the break; NZ finished 239-5 in their second innings, still 113 runs behind, when the captains shook hands; Daryl Mitchell 49 not out (186 balls) and Glenn Phillips 26 not out (126 balls) put on 63 for the sixth wicket; second and final Test begins Friday in Christchurch. RNZ/Reuters (24 Nov 2026, 'India draw feels like a win for Black Caps skipper Tom Latham'): Latham said the draw felt like a victory 'given the parlous positions' his team were in; India had reduced the home side to 70-5 just after lunch on day one before NZ recovered to post 368; Latham was dismissed by Jasprit Bumrah in the first over of each innings (a pair of ducks); his quote: 'I guess that's one that we've probably got away with'; New Zealand were top of the WTC standings before the Test, were overhauled by defending champions South Africa, and slipped to third behind Australia after the draw; the second India Test is followed by a tour of Australia and a home series against Sri Lanka ahead of the WTC final at The Oval in June (Latham helped NZ beat India in the 2021 final).
